ending: The novel ends in a cheap flat in the Rue de l'Homme Armé, in the summer of 1833. Jean Valjean has told Marius the truth about himself, been pushed gently out of Cosette's life, and stopped eating. He puts on his old workman's clothes, lays out the little mourning dress Cosette wore when he took her from Montfermeil, and lights the Bishop's candlesticks in broad daylight. Then he tries to write to her and cannot finish. Thénardier, of all people, saves the ending. He comes to sell Marius a scandal about Valjean, and the proof he brings shows the opposite: Valjean was M. Madeleine, Javert killed himself, and the man who carried Marius through the sewer was Valjean. Marius and Cosette reach him just in time. He tells Cosette her mother's name was Fantine, leaves her the candlesticks, blesses them both with his hands on their heads, and dies.

The death scene answers the first book of the novel. In 1815 Bishop Myriel gave a thief two silver candlesticks and told him he had bought his soul for God. Valjean has carried them through every name and every flight since. He dies by their light, saying he does not know whether the man who gave them to him is pleased with him. The reader knows the answer. Hugo gives the last image to an angel waiting in the dark for that soul. The chapter title says the same thing more plainly: 'A Night Behind Which There Is Day.'

The last revelations are cruel in their timing. Marius has spent months searching for the stranger who carried him out of the barricade, while that man sat in his house every evening and was quietly frozen out of it. Marius's coldness is not malice. He has decided that Valjean stole Madeleine's fortune and killed Javert. He is wrong on both counts, and he learns it only from the one person who really is a thief and a liar. Hugo lets the worst man in the book bring the truth, almost by accident. Then he sends Thénardier to America with Marius's money, where he becomes a slave-dealer. Evil is not punished at the end of this novel. It is paid off and goes elsewhere.

The final chapter is a single page. In a remote corner of Père-Lachaise, near the common grave, a plain stone without a name lies under a yew. Someone once wrote four lines on it in pencil: that he sleeps, that he lived despite a strange fate, and that he died when he lost his angel, as simply as night comes when day goes. Rain and dust have since rubbed them out. The man who was a number, then Madeleine, Leblanc, Fauchelevent and 'Monsieur Jean', ends with no name at all, as he asked. Hugo, who wrote twelve hundred pages, ends by letting the words fade.

Why does Valjean have to lose Cosette before he can die? The book's answer is that his last struggle is not with Javert or with poverty but with love. He wins Cosette's happiness by giving her up, first to Marius at the barricade and then in the slow retreat to the cold ground-floor room. His confession to Marius was owed to no one but his conscience. The ending rewards it only at the last minute, and only with the truth. That is the shape of the whole novel: goodness is costly and mostly unseen, and it is recognized late, if at all.

themes.text: The Bishop's mercy in the first book and Valjean's mercy to Javert at the barricade are the two hinges of the novel. Javert cannot survive the second. A man he hunted for years spared him, and he let that man go, so his belief that the law is always right falls apart and he drowns himself in the Seine. The law of the book is never wicked in itself. It is blind. It sends a man to the galleys for a loaf, and hounds Fantine for striking a man who pushed snow down her back. Mercy sees the person in front of it. Hugo leaves no doubt which of the two he thinks is higher.

Valjean's great moral crises, the night of 'A Tempest in a Skull' before Champmathieu's trial and the night after the wedding, end the same way: he gives himself up when nothing forces him to. The confession to Marius is the purest of them, since no one suspects him and no one is asking. Conscience in the book is not a feeling of guilt. It is the inner judge that will not let him enjoy a happiness built on a lie. It costs him Montreuil-sur-Mer and his freedom, and in the end Cosette. It is also the thing that makes him free.

The novel never solves poverty, and Hugo did not think a novel could. What it does is show what poverty does to people. Fantine sells her hair and her teeth. The Thénardiers turn misery into a trade. Gavroche lives in the plaster elephant of the Bastille. Éponine is twisted by hunger and is still capable of a great love. Hugo's preface says the book is needed as long as the degradation of man by poverty, the ruin of woman by hunger and the stunting of the child by darkness go unsolved. The ending does not cancel the debt. Cosette is rescued by one man's fortune, not by a reformed society.

The book holds many kinds of love side by side, and they test each other. Marius and Cosette's romance is ideal, chaste and a little absurd. Éponine loves without hope, and leads Marius to the barricade so they might die together. Valjean's love for Cosette is the deepest of all and has a jealous side: he reads her note in a mirror and hates the young man. He overcomes it, saves his rival through the sewers, and gives the couple everything. The end shows the cost. The happy lovers forget him, and he dies, as the doctor says, of having lost someone dear.

Hardly anyone in the novel is raised by the people who made them. Fantine has to leave Cosette with strangers. The Thénardiers prize their daughters and throw out their sons. Gavroche, unloved himself, takes in two lost little boys, who are his own brothers without his knowing it. Gillenormand cuts off his grandson and Georges Pontmercy can love his son only from behind a church pillar. Against all this stands Valjean, who becomes a father by choosing it. At his death he gives Cosette her mother's name, Fantine. The two parents the book began with meet at last in her.

The rising of June 1832 fails. Paris does not join it, the friends of the ABC die one by one, and Enjolras and Grantaire are shot side by side. Hugo refuses to call that failure meaningless. He separates a riot from an insurrection and admits that every blade has two edges. Then he treats the barricade as a step in the long march from night to day. Marius survives and joins the bourgeoisie, and the book's idea of progress moves from the barricade into conscience and education. That is where Hugo, an exile writing for a future republic, placed his hope.

Paris is a character in its own right, from the Gorbeau tenement and the Luxembourg to the Rue Plumet garden and the twisting streets around Saint-Merry. The city's last face is its underside. In the sewer, which Hugo calls the conscience of the city, nothing is disguised and everything confesses. Valjean carries Marius through it and comes up by the river, under Javert's eyes. The city that makes revolutions also abandons them, and in the end it hides an old man's grave in a far corner of Père-Lachaise.

Hugo's rule is that the only social danger is darkness and the only cure is light, by which he means teaching and conscience. The candlesticks are the novel's lamp. They pass from the Bishop to the thief, travel through every disguise, and light Valjean's deathbed in daylight. The sewer is the deepest night, and Valjean comes out of it holding Marius up. The last chapter title promises day behind the night, and the angel waits in a starless dark. The light given in the first book is still burning at the end.

Hugo sets small lives inside big events: Waterloo, the year 1817, the July Monarchy, the cholera and the rising of 1832. History moves people without their noticing. A scavenger stripping corpses at Waterloo becomes, to a dying colonel, a rescuer, and that mistake shapes Marius's life and nearly makes him spare a murderer. Hugo's digressions say the same thing in the open. The convent, the argot and the sewer belong to history as much as battles and kings do, and the historian of a society's depths has as grave a duty as the historian of its wars.

Valjean is a number at Toulon (24,601), then M. Madeleine, Urbain Fabre, M. Leblanc, Ultime Fauchelevent and finally 'Monsieur Jean'. Each name is a refuge, and each is lost. The Thénardiers use names as tools: Jondrette, Fabantou, Thénard, picked up and dropped as needed. Names are also kept from people. Cosette never knew her mother's name until her father's last hour. The book closes on a stone with no name at all and four pencilled lines the rain has washed away. The man who struggled for a self his name could not hold is remembered only by what he did.

interpretations.title: Saint or man?
interpretations.text: Some readers find Valjean too good, more an allegory of redemption than a person: the convict turned saint, Christ-like in the sewer, crucified slowly by Marius's coldness. Others point to how hard Hugo works to keep him human. He robs Petit-Gervais just after the Bishop's mercy, nearly lets Champmathieu go to the galleys in his place, hates Marius when he reads Cosette's note, and feels a 'frightful joy' at the thought of the boy's death. Read this way, his goodness is not a nature but a choice he keeps having to make again, often at night and alone.

interpretations.title: Javert: villain or tragic hero?
interpretations.text: Javert is no ordinary villain. He is honest, incorruptible and as hard on himself as on others; he even asks Madeleine to dismiss him for having falsely denounced him. Many critics see him as the book's true tragic figure, a man built entirely of one rule who is destroyed when mercy shows him the rule is not enough. His suicide chapter, 'Javert Derailed', is one of the boldest things in the novel: Hugo spends pages inside a mind that has no room for what has just happened to it. Adaptations from the 1935 film to the musical have tended to make him larger and more sympathetic still.

interpretations.title: Are the digressions the point?
interpretations.text: Waterloo, the convent of the Petit-Picpus, Parisian argot, the history of the sewers, the gamin of Paris: long stretches of the book pause the story. Many readers skip them, and some translators and editors have cut them. Hugo defended them as part of the design. His novel is about society, history and God as well as about Valjean, and he wanted the lives of his characters set against the forces that move them. Read closely, most digressions mirror the plot. Waterloo gives us Thénardier and Pontmercy, the convent prepares Valjean's refuge, and the sewer chapters build the stage for his descent with Marius.

interpretations.title: Marius, Cosette and the problem of the young
interpretations.text: Many readers find the young lovers the weakest part of the book. Cosette has little to do after childhood, and Marius is earnest, self-absorbed and quick to judge. Yet Hugo seems to know this. Marius's political journey from royalist to Bonapartist to something like a republican mirrors Hugo's own. His harsh judgement of Valjean is presented as a failure of understanding, which Hugo excuses but does not admire. Cosette's forgetfulness belongs to the happy. The book's sympathy, in the end, is with the old and the forgotten, not with the newlyweds.

interpretations.title: A political novel or a religious one?
interpretations.text: Les Misérables is both a call for social reform and a deeply religious book, though not a churchly one. Hugo attacks the death penalty, the treatment of convicts and the abandonment of the poor. He also builds the novel on a bishop's act of grace and ends it with an angel. Critics on the left found the religion sentimental; others, including Lamartine, found the politics dangerous. Hugo saw no conflict. For him progress and Providence were the same march, from evil to good and from night to day.

context.title: A book written across exile
context.text: Hugo began the novel in the mid-1840s under the working title Les Misères and had written much of it by February 1848, when revolution broke out and he set it aside for politics. After he opposed Louis-Napoléon's coup of December 1851, he went into exile, first in Brussels, then on Jersey, and from 1855 on Guernsey, at Hauteville House. He took the manuscript up again in 1860, after twelve years, and revised and greatly expanded it, adding much of the philosophy and history. He finished it in 1861, partly at Waterloo itself. It came out in 1862 from a Brussels publisher while its author was still in exile, and he did not return until the empire fell in 1870.

context.title: The June Rising of 1832
context.text: The barricade is real history. In the spring of 1832 Paris was hit by cholera and anger at the July Monarchy of Louis-Philippe. On 5 June the funeral of General Lamarque, a popular opposition figure, turned into an uprising. Republican students and workers held barricades in the old streets near Les Halles for about a day before the army crushed them; the last stand was around the cloister of Saint-Merry. Hugo was in Paris and was caught near the fighting. He places his barricade in the Rue de la Chanvrerie and invents the friends of the ABC, but the hopelessness, the silence of the city and the final assault follow the historical event closely.

context.title: Real models, a huge success and the Hapgood translation
context.text: Hugo drew on real people and things he saw. Bishop Myriel is based on Bishop Miollis of Digne. Valjean owes something to a convict named Pierre Maurin and to Vidocq, the convict who became a police chief. In 1841 Hugo saw a young man push snow down a prostitute's back and the woman arrested for fighting back, as Fantine is. The book was an immediate popular triumph across Europe and America, although many literary critics, among them Flaubert and Lamartine, were harsh. This companion follows Isabel F. Hapgood's 1887 American translation, which is close to the French and keeps the digressions. Some later versions, such as Norman Denny's (1976), moved or trimmed them.

questions: The Bishop says he has bought Valjean's soul for God. Was it bought in that moment, or did Valjean have to earn it over the rest of his life?
Why can Javert not live with having let Valjean go? Is his suicide an act of despair, of honesty, or both?
Valjean confesses to Marius when no one suspects him. Was it right to do so, given what it cost him and Cosette?
How fairly does Hugo treat Marius in the last book? Is his coldness to 'Monsieur Jean' forgivable?
Thénardier is never punished and ends as a slave-dealer in America. What does the book gain, or lose, by letting him go?
Which of the digressions (Waterloo, the convent, argot, the sewers) changed how you read the story, and which would you cut?
The rising of 1832 fails completely. Does the novel think the friends of the ABC died for nothing?
Valjean asks for a grave without a name. Why might that matter to him, after a life of so many names?
